questions.prompt: Nora is signed into A through a shared identity provider. What is known about B?

options.label: B’s local session remains separate and needs its own configured login flow.
Shared sign-in removes every local session.

questions.explanation: Provider-session reuse can reduce login interaction, but each application’s local session remains a separate configured object. One client cookie does not establish another application’s authorization.

questions.prompt: A token has a trusted signature but names another audience. Under the exercise’s policy, what follows?

options.label: Any trusted signature permits use by every client.
Only the token’s display name matters.
Reject it for this client despite the valid signature.

questions.explanation: Signature validity and intended audience are separate checks. The policy requires this registered client; a display name and trusted issuer signature cannot repair a mismatched audience.

questions.prompt: The client sent transaction nonce N but receives M. What follows?

options.label: Send M back as a replacement for the original transaction.
Reject the mismatch before using the returned tokens.
Ignore the nonce because the user is familiar.

questions.explanation: The returned nonce must match the one bound to this initiated transaction. Familiar identity and replacing stored state after the fact do not establish the required transaction continuity.

questions.prompt: A code exchange supplies a verifier but the authorization request had no challenge. What should happen?

options.label: Reject the exchange; a verifier cannot retroactively establish the missing challenge.
Accept any verifier as proof of safety.
Infer a challenge from the account name.

questions.explanation: The challenge belongs to the original authorization request. RFC 9700 requires downgrade protection here; an arbitrary verifier or account attribute does not establish that missing transaction binding.

questions.prompt: Nora has a valid local session with read permission on I9. May she refund I9?

options.label: Every authenticated user may refund every invoice.
PKCE itself grants invoice refund access.
Only if the resource’s current refund authorization check permits that action.

questions.explanation: Identity and code-exchange protection do not define object-action permission. The handler must enforce current refund authorization; read access and PKCE do not supply that separate grant.
